frontmatter.title: Compiling C Code on Linux/Unix Systems: A Practical Introduction

children.value: is a software tool that translates source code written in a high-level programming language, such as C, C++, or Fortran, into machine code or into a lower-level form that can eventually be executed by the CPU.
In High Performance Computing (HPC) environments, you will often find several compilers available. Each compiler may be optimized for specific hardware, standards, or performance goals.
: Default on most Unix systems. Open source and widely used in research and education.
: Optimized for Intel CPUs, offering high-performance vectorization and auto-parallelization.
: Fast, modular, and increasingly popular. Known for excellent compiler diagnostics.
: Targets CPU-GPU hybrid codes and includes OpenACC and CUDA support.
In a standard Linux distribution, the
compiler is almost always present. On macOS, you usually need to install the developer tools.
If you have access to a computing cluster, you can usually choose which compiler to use by loading the appropriate environment module, for example:

module load gcc
module load intel/2024
module load nvhpc
When you compile a C program, you convert human-readable source code into an executable binary.
For compiled languages such as C and Fortran, the typical process is:
source code → compiler → object file → linker → executable
